scenario: AITA - For not extending a specific invitation to two nieces for an annual family event that everyone is invited to? | Every year, on the last day of March, we gather as a family to celebrate my father-in-law’s life at a specific restaurant. He passed away many years ago, and that was his favorite place to eat. My mother-in-law foots the bill as part of the celebration and everyone in the family that can attend is always welcome. Sometimes people bring friends and it is never a big deal and we all celebrate a great man. This year, we had 3 of the 4 of my mother-in-law’s kids and their families come and had a wonderful time. My wife took a picture and posted it to social media to honor her dad. The unrepresented kid (I say kid loosely as she is over 50) took exception to this and flew off the handle because their family didn’t get an invitation and were purposely excluded. It is an open invitation, and she and all her children are adults with working phones. AITA for not reaching out to them and explicitly inviting them? Or should they know they are welcome (since they have been every other year) and take the initiative to just come? I didn’t get an invite and I showed up, so maybe IATA for a different reason.

prediction.raw: **0 (You're not the asshole)** **Why:** - **You are not the host.** The event is organized and funded by your mother-in-law, who explicitly stated it’s an "open invitation" for *all* family members. As a participant (not the decision-maker), it’s **not your responsibility** to individually invite anyone. - **"Open invitation" means no explicit outreach is required.** If the event is truly open to all family (as described), it’s reasonable to expect adults to know they’re welcome and take initiative to attend. Your own behavior proves this: you showed up without an invite, so the same logic applies to the nieces’ family. - **Social media post ≠ exclusion.** Your wife shared a photo *after* the event to honor her father. This was a celebration of the gathering that *happened*, not an invitation. The upset family member misinterpreted the post as a "private" event, but the issue lies with their assumption that they needed a direct invite to a public family gathering. - **The real problem is communication breakdown on their end.** If they’ve attended every year before, they should know the event is open. If they didn’t come this year, it’s likely due to their own scheduling, personal reasons, or a misunderstanding—not your fault. **Key takeaway:** - **Hosts handle invites; guests handle attendance.** Since your mother-in-law is the host, *she* should address any concerns about who was "missing." Your role was simply to attend and enjoy the event. - **If this becomes a recurring issue:** Suggest your mother-in-law sends a general family-wide reminder (e.g., "Everyone is welcome! Let me know if you can make it!") next year to avoid confusion. But *you* did nothing wrong here. > ️ **Final verdict:** **Not the asshole (0)**. The onus was on the family to know they were welcome and to RSVP themselves. Your actions were entirely appropriate.
